title: Prebuilt Cache Providers and Maturity
readerIntent: Choose a cache provider that matches topology and consistency needs.
summary: NodeCache is process-local reference behavior, Redis is a guarded distributed adapter, and Hazelcast is a fail-closed extension slot until a real adapter is supplied and qualified.

sections.heading: NodeCache
paragraphs: Useful for local development, a single process, or data that tolerates per-process copies. Restart clears it, and it cannot prove cross-node invalidation or strict distributed session semantics.

sections.heading: Redis
paragraphs: The distributed adapter is appropriate for shared channels only after live qualification of connection security, atomic operations, invalidation, failure behavior, capacity, recovery, and supported versions.

sections.heading: Hazelcast
paragraphs: The current slot must fail closed until a project or reusable provider implements the generic adapter contract and passes live cluster tests. Installed local software alone does not activate or qualify it.

sections.heading: Selection
items: Required TTL, atomic consume, prefix flush, serialization, and diagnostics.
Latency, payload size, availability, persistence expectations, and cost.

sections.heading: Maturity interpretation
items: A provider module or installed server does not prove adapter completeness.
Deterministic tests prove interface behavior, not network partitions or cluster recovery.
Local live tests prove one version and topology only.
Production qualification covers supported versions, security, failure, recovery, capacity, and operations.

sections.heading: Channel fit
paragraphs: NodeCache can serve low-risk process-local channels where independent copies and restart loss are acceptable. Redis can serve shared distributed channels after atomicity and invalidation qualification. Hazelcast requires a real generic adapter before any channel selects it.
Strict session, authentication, consume-once, or security decisions require stronger semantics than an ordinary performance cache.

sections.heading: Provider comparison evidence
items: Hit, miss, expiry, consume, serialization, and size behavior.
Startup outage, partition, reconnect, eviction, and restart.
TLS, credentials, least privilege, and secret rotation.
Load, memory, latency, topology, upgrade, and cost.

sections.heading: Safe activation
paragraphs: Only one provider is selected for a logical channel unless the capability explicitly defines multi-provider behavior. Enabling several adapters without routing rules creates inconsistent caches.
Provider changes include a namespace and invalidation plan so old entries cannot be interpreted under a new representation.

Treat a local installation as test infrastructure, not proof of production readiness. Record the adapter version, server version, topology, serialization format, security mode, and exercised failure cases so another operator can reproduce the documented qualification.
